q: A scanned contract PDF yields empty text from your parser. What is the right next step?
options: Switch to a larger embedding model
Run OCR (or a vision-based extractor) on the page images
why: Scanned PDFs contain images, not text, so OCR is needed. Chunking or embedding settings cannot fix missing text.

q: After a policy doc is edited, which approach keeps the index correct at lowest cost?
options: Compare content hashes, re-embed changed docs, and delete their stale chunks
why: Hash comparison plus delete-and-upsert limits work to what changed and prevents stale chunks. Appending alone leaves old text retrievable.

q: Which cleaning step most damages table-heavy documents?
options: Flattening tables to plain space-joined text
why: Flattening loses the column-to-value mapping, so numbers become ambiguous. Footers and whitespace are harmless noise to remove.

q: A fact is split across two adjacent chunks and never retrieved correctly. Which is the most direct mitigation?
options: Add modest chunk overlap or boundary-aware splitting
why: Overlap or sentence/paragraph-aware boundaries keep the fact whole in at least one chunk; the other options do not affect boundaries.

q: You must choose between 2,000-token and 300-token chunks for short FAQ lookup. What is the best reasoning?
options: Smaller chunks give sharper vectors for narrow questions; validate on labelled queries
Larger always wins because more context
Chunk size has no retrieval effect
why: Narrow factual queries match focused chunks; large chunks dilute the embedding. Still, the real answer comes from measuring on your eval set.

q: What is the main benefit of parent-child retrieval?
options: Precise matching on small chunks while giving the LLM larger context
why: Small children match accurately; returning the parent supplies the surrounding context for generation. It does not reduce index size.

q: Which chunking approach follows author-defined headings and code blocks?
why: Structural chunking uses document structure like headings, functions or tables. Fixed-size ignores it; semantic uses embedding similarity.

q: Which is a known weakness of dense embeddings?
options: Exact rare identifiers such as error codes
why: Opaque identifiers carry little semantic signal and get blurred; paraphrase and topical similarity are strengths.

q: You upgrade the embedding model for new documents only and keep old vectors. What happens?
options: Recall degrades because old and new vectors live in different spaces
why: Different models define incompatible spaces, so queries compare badly against one set. Re-embed everything or keep separate collections.

q: What is the best way to choose between candidate embedding models?
options: Pick the top public leaderboard model
Evaluate recall@k and MRR on labelled queries from your domain, weighing cost and latency
why: Leaderboards give a shortlist, but domain jargon, language and cost mean you must measure on your own data.

q: A 12k-token chunk is embedded with a 512-token model. What is the likely outcome?
options: Most content is silently truncated and not represented
The model splits it automatically with no loss
why: Inputs over the limit are cut, so the vector reflects only the start. Re-chunk to fit.

q: For unit-normalised vectors, which statement is true?
options: Euclidean ranks in the opposite order from cosine
Cosine and dot product rank identically
why: With unit length, cosine equals dot and L2 ordering matches, since squared L2 = 2 - 2cos.

q: Query is 'ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID after renewing'. Dense search returns generic SSL pages. Best improvement?
options: Add BM25 lexical matching via hybrid retrieval
why: Rare exact tokens are BM25's strength; hybrid recovers them. k or metric changes do not add lexical signal.

q: Semantic search always returns k results. Which consequence follows?
options: Irrelevant results can appear when nothing relevant exists, so thresholds or rerank scores are needed
why: Nearest neighbours exist even when far away; use thresholds/abstention.

q: Why implement brute-force search first?
options: It gives exact ground truth and teaches the mechanics
why: It is an exact baseline for measuring ANN recall and debugging, though not scalable.

q: A selective metadata filter applied after ANN top-10 returns just 1 result. What is the best fix?
options: Use pre/integrated filtering or oversample candidates
why: Post-filtering throws away most of the 10 candidates. Integrated filtering or oversampling keeps enough matches.

q: Which index typically gives best recall/latency but uses the most RAM?
why: HNSW's graph plus vectors live in memory; IVF-PQ compresses at some accuracy cost.

q: You must support deletes and edits to documents frequently. What is a sound pattern?
options: Upsert by deterministic ID, delete by doc_id, and schedule compaction/monitor recall
Store vectors only in the app cache
why: Deterministic IDs and doc-level deletes keep the index consistent; compaction reclaims tombstones.

q: Why is ANN acceptable for RAG despite being approximate?
options: Small recall loss rarely changes answers and rerankers can fix ordering
why: Embeddings are fuzzy anyway; high-recall ANN plus reranking gives near-exact quality at low latency.

q: When is pgvector a good starting choice?
options: You already run Postgres and have up to millions of vectors
why: It leverages existing ops, transactions and joins at moderate scale; dedicated engines suit larger scale.

q: Which query most favours BM25 over dense retrieval?
options: 'How do I get my money back?'
why: A rare exact token sequence matches lexically; the others are paraphrase-style queries suited to dense.

q: Why is RRF a good default for fusion?
options: It uses ranks, so incompatible score scales do not matter
It removes the need for retrieval
why: Rank-based fusion sidesteps score-scale differences and requires almost no tuning.

q: Your hybrid system shows no gain over dense alone. Most informative first step?
options: Break down eval results by query type and check lexical tokenisation and candidate depth
why: You need to see whether the queries even contain lexical-type needs and whether the lexical side is functioning.

q: BM25 length normalisation exists to...
options: Avoid unfairly favouring long documents with more term occurrences
why: Longer docs naturally contain more term hits; b scales that effect.

q: Gold passage is not in the top-k at all. Which stage failed?
why: Missing evidence from the retrieved set is a retrieval failure; generation cannot use what it was not given.

q: Which is the best case for NOT using RAG?
options: Large private corpus that changes daily
A 10-page static FAQ that fits in the prompt
why: Small static knowledge can simply go in the prompt; RAG adds complexity without benefit.

q: What does RAG primarily provide compared with fine-tuning?
options: Current, private, citable knowledge at query time
why: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour; RAG supplies knowledge you can update and cite.

q: A question asks for the total number of contracts signed last year across 50k docs. RAG top-k likely...
options: Misses most documents; use structured data/aggregation instead
why: Top-k samples a few chunks and cannot aggregate over everything; use SQL or map-reduce style processing.

q: Where should the user question go in the assembled prompt, typically?
why: Placing the question after the context takes advantage of stronger attention at the end and keeps instructions clear.

q: Retrieved documents contain text telling the model to ignore its instructions. Best defence?
options: Delimit context as untrusted data, instruct not to follow it, and validate outputs
why: Prompt injection is mitigated by data/instruction separation and defence in depth.

q: Which signal best supports abstaining?
options: All retrieved scores below a calibrated threshold
High reranker score for top chunk
why: Low calibrated scores indicate weak evidence; thresholds must be tuned on labelled data.

q: Raising k from 5 to 25 hurts answers. Most plausible reason?
options: Noise and positional effects bury relevant passages
why: More context adds distraction and lost-in-the-middle effects; rerank and narrow instead.

q: Why build the baseline pipeline by hand first?
options: It shows every stage and gives a measurable baseline
why: Understanding and baselines make later frameworks and improvements debuggable.

q: Why use a cross-encoder only on a shortlist?
options: It needs one forward pass per query-passage pair, too slow for the whole corpus
why: Cross-encoders are accurate but not precomputable; they are applied to the first-stage candidates.

q: Gold chunk is absent from the top-50 first-stage candidates. A reranker will...
options: Not help; improve recall via hybrid, chunking or query transformation
why: Rerankers reorder candidates; they cannot add missing ones.

q: Which is the best reason a reranker lets you send fewer chunks to the LLM?
options: It improves precision of the top few so less noise is needed
why: Better ordering makes a small final k sufficient, cutting tokens and distraction.

q: Latency is critical and reranker service sometimes times out. Best design?
options: Timeout with fallback to first-stage ordering
why: A timeout fallback preserves availability with graceful quality degradation.

q: A user asks 'what about the premium plan?' after discussing pricing. Best first step?
options: Condense it with chat history into a standalone query
why: The follow-up lacks context; a condense/rewrite step makes it retrievable.

q: What is HyDE's retrieval signal?
options: An embedding of an LLM-written hypothetical answer
why: HyDE embeds a hypothetical answer, which resembles documents, and uses it only for retrieval.

q: RAG-Fusion merges per-variant lists with...
why: RRF fuses by rank, avoiding score calibration problems across lists.

q: Which query should you most likely NOT rewrite?
options: 'ORA-00942 table or view does not exist'
why: Exact error identifiers should stay verbatim so lexical matching works.

q: Ambiguous query where interpretations give different answers and a wrong answer is costly. Best behaviour?
options: Ask a brief clarifying question or present each interpretation
why: Clarifying or covering interpretations avoids confident wrong answers.

q: A response cites a real document that does not actually state the claim. This shows...
options: Citations are not grounding; support must be verified
why: A citation is a pointer; verifying entailment is what establishes support.

q: What is a cheap programmatic check for citation validity?
options: Require a quote per claim and string-match it in the cited chunk
why: Quote matching catches fabricated or non-supporting citations.

q: Two retrieved policies disagree. Best answer behaviour?
options: Present both with citations and dates, flagging the conflict
why: Surfacing the conflict preserves honesty; silently resolving it hides risk.

q: In a medical RAG, which abstention tuning is appropriate?
options: Favour refusal, accepting more false refusals, with human escalation
why: High-stakes domains prioritise avoiding false answers over coverage.

q: Why mark synthesis separately from evidence?
options: Users and checkers can tell sourced facts from model inference
why: Separation clarifies what is verifiable versus inferred and enables different checks.

q: Which technique best targets 'sometimes retrieval returns irrelevant docs and we can't tell when'?
why: Grading retrieval and routing to a fallback addresses unreliable retrieval; chunk size or temperature do not detect it.

q: A question needs facts from a document found only after reading another. Best fit?
options: Multi-hop or iterative retrieval with decomposition
why: Dependent hops require sequential retrieval using intermediate findings.

q: What does Self-RAG's reflection tokens represent?
options: Model-generated judgments about retrieval need, relevance, support and usefulness
why: They let the model critique passages and its own output, controlling retrieval and selection.

q: Corpus-wide 'what are the main themes across all reports?' Which approach fits?
options: Graph RAG global query using community summaries
why: Top-k samples a few passages; community summaries enable corpus-level synthesis.

q: Adaptive RAG's main benefit is...
options: Using the cheapest adequate strategy per query to save cost and latency
why: Routing avoids heavy pipelines on easy questions while still handling hard ones.

q: Your team wants to add three advanced RAG techniques at once. Best advice?
options: Add one at a time driven by categorised failures and measure ablations
why: Ablation shows what helps; stacking hides regressions and costs.

q: In LlamaIndex-style vocabulary, which component builds the prompt from retrieved nodes and calls the LLM?
why: The synthesizer handles prompt assembly and generation; the retriever only fetches nodes.

q: After porting to a framework, answers differ from your baseline. First check?
options: Compare chunking, retrieved ids and the final prompt using tracing
why: Defaults for chunk size, prompts and retrievers are the usual cause; inspecting each stage locates it.

q: Which is a legitimate reason to prefer thin hand-built orchestration?
options: Need stable, explicit, testable control of prompts and flow in a long-lived service
why: Control and stability matter for core services; libraries can still be used for commodity pieces.

q: Reranking in a framework pipeline is typically configured as...
options: A postprocessor over a wide retrieval result, keeping a smaller top_n
why: Retrieve widely, then rerank and cut to a small set before synthesis.

q: A born-digital PDF extracts cleanly but a scanned sibling does not. What distinguishes the two?
options: Scanned pages are images and need OCR; born-digital already has text and structure
Scanned PDFs need a larger embedder only
OCR is required for every PDF
why: OCR is for page images. Running it on born-digital text wastes money and can smash tables you already had.

q: A document is deleted from the source system but still answers in RAG. What ingest step was skipped?
options: Tombstoning or deleting that doc's chunks (and graph edges) in the index
why: Deletes are first-class. Incremental ingest that only upserts leaves stale chunks retrievable.

q: A pricing table is split mid-row by a 512-token cutter. What should the chunker do?
options: Keep cutting at 512 no matter what
Treat the table (or row groups with a repeated header) as an atomic unit
Embed the whole PDF as one vector
why: Half a row is not a fact. Bust the size cap a bit or split on row groups, not through a cell.

q: How do you pick a starting chunk size in an interview?
options: The largest window the chat model has
Start from the embedder's useful length, measure recall, then adjust overlap
why: Size is an eval knob. Begin from the embedding model's useful length, then measure.

q: A teammate doubles embedding dimensions 'for quality' on a 20M-vector corpus. What do you check first?
options: Whether ANN RAM and query cost rose enough to erase any recall gain — higher dims are not free
Whether the chat model window grew
Whether BM25 needs the same dimension
why: Dimensionality is a storage and ANN cost. Quality is not automatic; measure before you buy RAM.

q: An instruction-tuned embedder expects a query prefix and you omit it at query time. Likely result?
options: Collapsed recall because queries and docs no longer sit in the same trained protocol
why: Prefix mismatch is a silent recall hole. Match the model card on both ingest and query.

q: You built an L2 index on a cosine-trained embedder. What do you do?
options: Tune k until it looks fine
Rebuild with the matching metric (or normalise and use IP if that is the cosine path)
Lower ef to hide the mismatch
why: A wrong operator is a silent ranking bug. Rebuild; do not tune k on the wrong geometry.

q: The user asks for policies that are not about refunds. Dense search still returns the refund FAQ. What failed?
options: Cosine cannot be used for text
Semantic search is weak on negation (and often on exact ids and recency) — add lexical or a filter
why: Negation, identifiers, and recency are the usual semantic-search misses. Say what you add next: BM25 or a hard filter.

q: A tiny tenant always gets 0 ANN hits; brute-force finds their 20 docs. What do you suspect first?
options: Filter timing (pre vs post) emptying the graph neighbourhood — or the need for a per-tenant index
why: Tight filters plus naive HNSW is a classic empty. Check the engine's filter rule before swapping embedders.

q: Brute-force finds a chunk; default-ef ANN misses it. First knob?
options: Raise ef or nprobe and re-measure recall vs p95
why: ef/nprobe are product knobs on a recall-latency curve. Do not start with a new embedder.

q: Dense-only recall is 0.95; hybrid is 0.95 at +60ms. What do you do?
options: Drop the dead channel — it is only adding latency
Add raw BM25 to cosine without calibration
why: If one channel already has high recall, the other is a bill. Ablate and delete.

q: BM25 and the vector index used different chunk ids for the same span. What breaks at fusion?
options: RRF (or any merge) cannot treat them as one object, so the span competes with itself and citations fork
why: Shared chunk ids are the hybrid contract. Different ids make fusion a join from hell.

q: A PM wants RAG so the bot sounds more confident. What do you say?
options: RAG is not a style tool — ask which private or changing facts must be cited
why: RAG supplies facts, not tone. Style is parametric or a system prompt.

q: The answer is fluent and wrong. The assembled prompt does not contain the gold span. Which side failed?
options: Retrieval — raise k or fix chunk/query/filters, not the chat model first
The vector metric cannot be cosine
why: If the span was never in the prompt, it is a retrieve miss. Fluency is not evidence.

q: The model cites [7] and you only sent sources [1]–[4]. What should the checker do?
options: Reject the citation (and maybe abstain) — it is an unretrieved id
Fetch random doc 7 from the corpus
Raise k to 7 next time only
why: Never accept a title or id you did not retrieve. That is invented grounding.

q: Eight assembled chunks are overlap slices of one paragraph; the gold is in another doc. First fix?
options: Dedupe / diversify before assemble so k is not a lie
why: Near-duplicates waste the window. Raise unique-doc count before you raise k.

q: First-stage recall@4 is 0.94 and rerank lifts it to 0.94 at +150ms. What do you do?
options: Skip the reranker until an eval proves lift that pays for the latency
why: Skip is the default when the first stage already ranks well. Always-on is a latency leak.

q: How do you place a reranker in an interview, including the measurement?
options: Send 50 chunks to the LLM and hope
Retrieve about 50, rerank about 8, send about 4 — and measure extra latency and quality
why: 50 → 8 → 4 is the sketch. The grade is that you measure the extra latency, not that you name a vendor.

q: HyDE is on for query INC-4419 and you retrieve a generic incident essay. What failed?
options: HyDE drifted off the identifier — skip it on precise queries and keep raw BM25
The ticket id is too short to embed
why: Hypothetical documents become prose and miss codes. Do not HyDE identifier queries.

q: After a prompt tweak, model calls per request doubled and quality did not. What do you check?
options: Whether rewrite/multi-query started firing on easy lookups — cap and skip those
why: Each transform is a billed call. A router and a cap belong in the budget, not only the final generate.

q: Why prefer quote-then-answer over answer-then-cite?
options: Writing the answer first invites invented sources to decorate it
Answer-then-cite is faster so it must be better
why: Extract spans first, then answer inside them. Answer-first is how titles get invented.

q: The model sets answer to probably 14 days and insufficient_evidence true. What do you render?
options: Both, so the user has options
Abstain only — dual-filled is a generate failure
why: A required abstain path beats a hedged paragraph. Do not show the leftover number.

q: Gold is never in the top-50 and the team adds Self-RAG reflection tokens. What should they fix instead?
options: Retrieve (chunk, hybrid, query). Reflection cannot promote a span that never arrived
why: Pick the variant from the failure. A retrieve miss is not a reflection miss.

q: Why is Graph RAG a poor week-one choice on a new corpus?
options: Entity graphs need extract, resolve, deletes, and summaries — staff ingest first; start with chunks
Vector search is illegal once a graph exists
why: Graphs are a second pipeline. Do not start there; try hops if a relation question fails.

q: After a LlamaIndex port the model uses outside knowledge your code never allowed. Where do you look first?
options: The hidden default prompt — dump the final assembled messages
why: Frameworks hide prompts. A default helpful-assistant line can undo your grounding rule.

q: The framework demo looks nicer but answers the uncovered fixture question. Ship it?
options: Only if the CEO likes the logo
No — it lost the abstain rule; fix or keep the hand-built generate path
why: Parity means the same fixture still abstains and still cites quote-plus-id. A demo that loses that is a fail.
